# AGENTS.md — shipfree

Repository guide for coding agents working on this repository.

## What this repository is

A single **Agent Skill** (`shipfree`) plus the harness that keeps its
numbers true. The skill teaches an AI agent how to deploy an AI service on
a free tier. The harness verifies every limit it quotes against the
platform's own documentation.

## The one rule

**Never hand-edit a limit.**

The limit tables inside `.agents/skills/shipfree/SKILL.md` are generated.
The source of truth is `limits.json`. To change a number:

```bash
python harness/fetch_limits.py --refresh   # pull the upstream docs
python harness/check_limits.py              # see what drifted
# edit limits.json with the new upstream value
python harness/render_skill.py              # regenerate the tables
python harness/render_skill.py --check      # confirm it is in sync
```

Editing the table directly is reverted by the next render and will fail CI.

## Layout

```
.agents/skills/shipfree/SKILL.md   the canonical skill (source of truth)
.opencode/skills/shipfree/         copy for opencode; kept byte-identical
.cursor/rules/shipfree.mdc         always-on context for Cursor
.clinerules/, .kiro/steering/       always-on context for other harnesses
.github/copilot-instructions.md    always-on context for Copilot
.claude-plugin/, .codex-plugin/    plugin manifests per harness
.agents/plugins/marketplace.json   the agents-standard marketplace entry

limits.json                        the single source of truth for every limit
harness/fetch_limits.py            fetch upstream docs, parse limit tables
harness/check_limits.py            compare limits.json against upstream
harness/render_skill.py            regenerate the skill's tables from limits.json
templates/                         deployable starting points
```

## Commands

```bash
make check        # everything CI runs
make limits       # refresh and check the limits
make render       # regenerate the skill tables
make test         # unit tests
```

## Conventions

- Python 3.10+, standard library only for the harness. No dependencies, so
  it runs anywhere and never needs a lockfile.
- Conventional Commits for the commit subject, because the history is the
  advertisement.
- Every asserted limit needs a `doc_label` where upstream puts it in a
  table, so a renamed or removed limit is reported as drift instead of
  passing silently.
- If you add a limit, add it in the same commit as the check that proves it.

## Do not

- Do not add a number that is not verified against upstream. If it cannot be
  verified, it belongs in prose, not in `limits.json`.
- Do not copy the skill into a second location without updating
  `tests/test_manifests.py`, which asserts every copy is byte-identical.
- Do not claim a limit in the README that is not in `limits.json`.

# shipfree — ship an AI service for free

Deploying an AI service is not hard. Deploying one that stays free while
people actually use it is hard, because the limits that decide whether it
stays free are scattered across half a dozen pricing pages, and they change
without notice.

This skill encodes the limits that matter, verified against the upstream
documentation, and the architecture that fits inside them.

**The core insight:** a free tier is not a smaller version of a paid tier.
It is a different shape. Some work fits in the free shape beautifully —
streaming a model response costs almost no CPU because the time spent
waiting on a socket is not CPU time. Other work cannot fit at all, no matter
how you arrange it. Know which is which before writing code.

---

## Step 0 — pick the platform

Do this before writing a line of code. The platform determines the
architecture, and the architecture determines everything else.

<!-- limits:begin platform_matrix -->
| Platform | Best for | WebSockets | Streaming | Card required | Cold start |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cloudflare Workers | Streaming AI APIs and realtime agents that must stay free at volume | yes, via Durable Objects | yes, native | no | none |
| Vercel | Next.js front ends and quick API routes | no on serverless functions | yes on the Edge runtime | no | yes |
| Hugging Face Spaces | Public model demos with a Gradio or Docker UI | limited | yes | no | sleeps after inactivity |
| Render | Long-running containers that need real sockets | yes | yes | yes | spins down when idle |
| Fly.io | Container workloads placed close to users | yes | yes | yes | no |
<!-- limits:end platform_matrix -->

**Default to Cloudflare Workers.** It is the only one of these with no cold
starts, no credit card requirement, free egress, and — decisively — a
Durable Objects tier that supports WebSockets and gives 30 seconds of CPU
per request instead of 10 milliseconds. If the workload is anything realtime
or anything stateful, that single difference settles it.

Use **Vercel** when the deliverable is a Next.js front end and the API is
an afterthought. Use **Hugging Face Spaces** when the point is to publish a
model demo, not to run a service.

---

## The limits that actually bite

Everything below was read from the platform's own documentation. It is not
a summary of a blog post; it is checked by a harness that fails CI when
upstream changes.

### Workers — the 10 ms rule

<!-- limits:begin workers -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| requests per day | 100,000/day — Resets at 00:00 UTC. Exceeding it returns Cloudflare error 1027. You can choose fail-open or fail-closed routing. |
| cpu time per invocation | 10 ms — The single most important number on this page, and the reason most AI workloads do not belong in a free Worker. The paid plan allows 5 minutes. |
| memory | 128 MB |
| subrequests per invocation | 50 — Subrequests to internal services (KV, D1, R2) have their own, larger budget of 1,000. |
| simultaneous outgoing connections | 6 — Relevant when proxying to several model APIs at once. |
| environment variables | 64/Worker — 5 KB per value. |
| worker size | 64 MiB |
| worker startup time | 1 second |
| workers per account | 100 |
| cron triggers per account | 5 |
| request body size | 100 MB — Set by the Cloudflare account plan, not by the Workers plan. |
| response body size | No enforced limit — Response body size is not capped by the Workers plan. |
<!-- limits:end workers -->

**10 ms of CPU is not "10 ms of wall clock".** Time spent waiting on a
network socket is not CPU time. So `await fetch("https://api.gemini...")`
costs almost nothing even when the model takes eight seconds to answer.
What *does* cost CPU is work: JSON parsing, string manipulation, crypto,
serialisation.

The consequence is concrete:

```ts
// Wrong. Buffers the whole response, then parses a large JSON body.
// A multi-megabyte response will blow the 10 ms budget.
const res = await fetch(url, { headers });
const data = await res.json();
return Response.json(data);

// Right. Piping the body through costs almost no CPU.
return new Response(res.body, {
  headers: { "content-type": "text/event-stream" },
});
```

Stream. Do not buffer. Parse only what you must.

### Durable Objects — the escape hatch

<!-- limits:begin durable_objects -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| max classes per account | 100 (Free) — Workers Paid allows 500. |
| storage per account | 5GB (Free) — Unlimited on Workers Paid. Storage is measured in GB (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes), not GiB. |
| storage per durable object | 10 GB |
| number of objects | Unlimited — Within an account or of a given class. |
| cpu per request | 30 seconds (default) — This is the escape hatch from the 10 ms Worker limit: every incoming request or WebSocket message resets the CPU budget to 30 seconds, configurable up to 5 minutes of active CPU time. |
| websocket message size | 32 MiB — Applies to received messages only. |
| key value size | 2 MB — Key and value combined. |
| free tier reset | Daily free limits reset at 00:00 UTC — Free-tier Durable Object limits are daily, not monthly. |
| included requests per month | 1,000,000 — The included allocation on the Workers Paid plan. |
| included duration gb s per month | 400,000 GB-s — Duration is billed in GB-seconds: seconds multiplied by memory in GB. |
| price per million requests | $0.15 — Charged beyond the included allocation on Workers Paid. |
| pending io holds memory | 15 minutes — A pending I/O operation keeps the object resident, and billable, for up to 15 minutes. |
<!-- limits:end durable_objects -->

**Rule of thumb: if a request needs more than 10 ms of CPU, it belongs in a
Durable Object.** That covers stateful sessions, WebSocket servers, anything
doing real computation, and every realtime agent.

**Use the WebSocket Hibernation API.** A hibernating Durable Object is
evicted from memory between messages and restored on the next one, which
removes the duration charge for an idle agent session. An agent that waits
ten seconds for the user to speak is idle most of the time — hibernate it.

### D1 — the query budget

<!-- limits:begin d1 -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| databases per account | 10 (Free) — Workers Paid allows 50,000. |
| max database size | 500 MB (Free) — Workers Paid allows 10 GB. |
| max storage per account | 5 GB (Free) — Workers Paid allows 1 TB. |
| queries per worker invocation | 50 (Free) — Workers Paid allows 1,000. This is the D1-specific budget: a free Worker may only issue 50 D1 queries per request, so batch reads into a single call instead of looping. |
| time travel retention | 7 days — Point-in-time recovery window. Workers Paid allows 30 days. |
| max row size | 2,000,000 bytes (2 MB) — Maximum string, BLOB or table row size. |
| max sql statement length | 100,000 bytes (100 KB) |
| max bound parameters | 100 |
| max query duration | 30 seconds |
| max restore operations | 10 restores per 10 minutes — Per database. |
<!-- limits:end d1 -->

Fifty queries per invocation is the number that catches people. A loop that
reads twenty conversations one at a time is already at 40% of the budget
before it does anything else.

```ts
// Wrong: N round trips, each one counting against the 50-query budget.
const rows = [];
for (const id of ids) {
  rows.push(await env.DB.prepare("SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?").bind(id).first());
}

// Right: one statement, one round trip.
const { results } = await env.DB.prepare(
  `SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (${ids.map(() => "?").join(",")})`
).bind(...ids).all();
```

### KV — reads are cheap, writes are not

<!-- limits:begin kv -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| reads per day | 100,000 reads per day |
| writes to different keys per day | 1,000 writes per day — The asymmetry with reads is the trap: reading a cached value is cheap, persisting state is not. Use KV as a cache, not as a database. |
| writes to same key | 1 per second — Applies to every plan. |
| storage per account | 1 GB |
| storage per namespace | 1 GB |
| value size | 25 MiB |
| key size | 512 bytes |
| operations per invocation | 1000 |
| namespaces per account | 1,000 |
| minimum cache ttl | 30 seconds — The smallest value you can pass to cacheTtl. |
<!-- limits:end kv -->

One thousand writes per day, and one write per second to the same key.
Any design where a Durable Object writes conversation state to KV on every
turn will hit the per-second ceiling within a minute of real traffic. Keep
session state inside the Durable Object, and use KV only for things you
read far more often than you write.

### R2 — free egress

<!-- limits:begin r2 -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| storage | 10 GB-month / month — Billed on the average peak storage per day across the billing period. Standard storage only. |
| class a operations | 1 million requests / month — List, Put, Copy and similar metadata operations. |
| class b operations | 10 million requests / month — Get and similar read operations. |
| egress | Free — The reason to prefer R2 over S3 on a free tier: there is no egress charge at all. |
| infrequent access storage | does not apply to Infrequent Access storage — The free tier covers Standard storage only. |
<!-- limits:end r2 -->

Free egress is the quiet superpower. Serving user uploads or model output
from R2 through a Worker costs nothing per byte served, where the same
traffic from S3 does not.

### Queues — the only place with real CPU

<!-- limits:begin queues -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| queues per account | 10,000 per account |
| message size | 128 KB — Around 100 bytes of that is internal metadata. |
| message retries | 100 |
| max consumer batch size | 100 messages |
| max send batch | 100 (or 256KB in total) |
| per queue throughput | 5,000 messages per second |
| message retention | Configurable up to 14 days |
| per queue backlog | 25GB |
| concurrent consumer invocations | 250 push-based only |
| consumer wall clock duration | 15 minutes |
| consumer cpu time | Configurable to 5 minutes — A queue consumer gets far more CPU time than an ordinary Worker. Run heavy work here rather than in the request path. |
| visibility timeout | 12 hours — Pull-based queues. |
| delay seconds | 24 hours — When sending or retrying. |
<!-- limits:end queues -->

A queue consumer gets **5 minutes of CPU** against a Worker's 10 ms. That
is a 30,000x difference. Anything heavy — embedding a batch of documents,
scraping and summarising a feed, transcoding media — belongs in a queue
consumer, not in the request handler and not in a Durable Object.

### Workers AI — inference with no API key

<!-- limits:begin workers_ai -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| free neurons per day | 10,000 Neurons per day — Resets at 00:00 UTC. Exceeding it fails further operations. |
| price per 1000 neurons | $0.011 per 1,000 Neurons — On the Workers Paid plan, above the free allocation. |
| text generation requests per minute | 300 requests per minute — Unless the model requires the Workers Paid plan. |
| embeddings requests per minute | 3000 requests per minute — The bge-large-en-v1.5 model is limited to 1500. |
| summarization requests per minute | 1500 requests per minute |
| image to text requests per minute | 720 requests per minute |
| asr requests per minute | 720 requests per minute |
| object detection requests per minute | 3000 requests per minute |
| text classification requests per minute | 2000 requests per minute |
| paid only models | @cf/moonshotai/kimi-k2.6, @cf/moonshotai/kimi-k2.7-code, @cf/zai-org/glm-5.2, @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3, @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash, @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731, @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017, and @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-pro-0813 — These require a Workers Paid plan or prepaid AI Gateway credits, so they are not available on a strictly free account. The list is asserted verbatim so that adding or removing a model is reported as drift. |
<!-- limits:end workers_ai -->

Workers AI is the fastest possible path to a working AI service: no
provider account, no API key, no card. Bind it and call it.

```ts
export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env) {
    const response = await env.AI.run(
      "@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct",
      { messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Hello" }] }
    );
    return Response.json(response);
  },
};
```

---

## The workflow

Work through these in order. Each step has a decision point, and each
decision point has one right answer for a free tier.

### 1. Write down what is actually free

Before anything else, name the four numbers that will decide success:

- **Requests per day** the service must survive
- **CPU per request** the work needs
- **State that must persist** and how much of it
- **Realtime or not** — this decides Durable Objects

If the CPU number exceeds 10 ms, you are done: use a Durable Object or a
queue consumer. No amount of cleverness changes that.

### 2. Scaffold

```bash
npm create cloudflare@latest my-ai-service
cd my-ai-service
npx wrangler login
```

Pin the runtime and set the compatibility date so a future Workers release
cannot silently change behaviour:

```toml
# wrangler.toml
name = "my-ai-service"
main = "src/index.ts"
compatibility_date = "2026-10-22"
compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"]
```

### 3. Add the bindings you will actually use

Only add what you use. Every binding costs part of a budget.

```toml
[[d1_databases]]
binding = "DB"
database_name = "my-ai-service"
database_id = "<created by wrangler d1 create my-ai-service>"

[[r2_buckets]]
binding = "FILES"
bucket_name = "my-ai-service-files"

[[kv_namespaces]]
binding = "CACHE"
id = "<created by wrangler kv namespace create CACHE>"

[[queues.producers]]
binding = "TASKS"
queue = "my-ai-service-tasks"

[[queues.consumers]]
queue = "my-ai-service-tasks"
max_batch_size = 100
max_batch_timeout = 5

[[durable_objects.bindings]]
name = "SESSIONS"
class_name = "Session"

[[migrations]]
tag = "v1"
new_classes = ["Session"]

[ai]
binding = "AI"
```

### 4. Put the API key somewhere safe

```bash
npx wrangler secret put GEMINI_API_KEY
```

Secrets are encrypted at rest and are not readable from the dashboard. Never
put a key in a `define:` block, an env var checked into git, or the
frontend bundle. If the browser needs to call a model directly, proxy
through a Worker instead of exposing a key.

### 5. Stream the response

```ts
async function streamModel(prompt: string, apiKey: string): Promise<Response> {
  const upstream = await fetch(GEMINI_URL, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json", "x-goog-api-key": apiKey },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      contents: [{ parts: [{ text: prompt }] }],
      generationConfig: { maxOutputTokens: 512 },
    }),
  });

  if (!upstream.ok || !upstream.body) {
    return new Response("upstream error", { status: 502 });
  }

  // Pipe. Do not buffer, do not parse.
  return new Response(upstream.body, {
    headers: {
      "content-type": "text/event-stream",
      "cache-control": "no-cache",
    },
  });
}
```

### 6. Add auth before you add features

An unauthenticated AI endpoint is a gift to someone else. Put it behind a
shared secret checked in the Worker, and put the secret in a Durable Object
or KV only if you need per-user state.

```ts
function authorized(request: Request, env: Env): boolean {
  const header = request.headers.get("authorization") ?? "";
  return header === `Bearer ${env.API_TOKEN}`;
}
```

### 7. Rate-limit before you are rate-limited

Two enforcement points, and they catch different abuse:

- **Cloudflare WAF rate-limiting rules** for per-IP floods at the edge
- **Application-level counters** for per-key or per-account quotas

For an application-level counter on a free tier, keep it in a Durable
Object rather than KV — KV allows one write per second to the same key,
which a burst will exceed immediately.

### 8. Move slow work off the request path

```ts
// In the request handler: enqueue and return.
await env.TASKS.send({ jobId, kind: "summarise" });

// In the queue consumer: do the heavy thing.
export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env): Promise<Response> {
    const batch = await request.json() as MessageBatch<Task>;
    for (const message of batch.messages) {
      await summarise(message.body);
      message.ack();
    }
    return new Response("ok");
  },
};
```

### 9. Watch the budget, not the deployment

A free tier does not fail loudly. It silently returns 1027 at 00:00 UTC, or
starts rejecting writes, and you find out from a user. Check the Workers
dashboard for request counts and CPU, and set a cron trigger to alert
yourself.

```toml
[triggers]
crons = ["0 * * * *"]
```

### 10. Verify it is still free

Before you call it done, check the four numbers again against real usage:

- Requests per day, measured
- CPU per request, measured
- Storage, measured
- Writes to the same key, measured

A deployment that is free on day one and bills you on day two is worse than
one that never shipped.

---

## Traps

**Buffering a streaming response.** The single most common mistake. It
turns a 10 ms budget into a multi-second one and breaks streaming for the
user. Pipe the body.

**Treating CPU time as wall-clock time.** Waiting on a socket is free. A
`while` loop over a large array is not. `JSON.parse` of a multi-megabyte
body is not.

**Using KV as a database.** One thousand writes per day and one write per
second per key. Use D1.

**Issuing D1 queries in a loop.** Fifty per invocation. Batch them.

**Running heavy work in the request handler.** Move it to a queue consumer
and get 5 minutes of CPU instead of 10 ms.

**Ignoring hibernation for realtime sessions.** An agent session that sits
idle between turns is billed for the whole session. Hibernation removes
that.

**Putting a provider API key in the frontend.** It is in the bundle, it is
public, and it will be used by someone else. Proxy through a Worker.

**Exposing a Durable Object class per user.** You get 100 classes on the
free tier, not 100,000 objects. Use one class, one object per user id.

**Assuming the free tier will last.** Verify the limits against the live
documentation before you quote a number to anyone. This skill's own limits
are checked by a harness in CI; do the same for anything you assert.

**Shipping without a README.** A deployment someone cannot run is not a
deployment. Write the setup steps, the environment variables, and one
working example.

---

## Templates

Working, deployable starting points live in `templates/`:

- `templates/streaming-proxy/` — a Worker that streams a model response and
  enforces a shared token
- `templates/agent-api/` — Worker + D1 + Durable Object session + queue
  consumer, the full stack for a realtime agent

Copy one, change one thing, deploy it, and you have a working service.

## Verifying a deployment

```bash
npx wrangler deploy --dry-run    # what would be uploaded
npx wrangler deploy              # ship it
npx wrangler tail                # live logs
```

## Keeping this skill honest

The limit tables in this skill are generated from `limits.json`, and
`limits.json` is verified against the platform's own documentation source by
`harness/check_limits.py`. If a limit changes upstream, CI fails and the
drift is reported with the upstream text and the asserted value side by
side.

Run it locally:

```bash
python harness/fetch_limits.py --refresh
python harness/check_limits.py
python harness/render_skill.py
```

If you find a stale number, do not edit the table above. Fix `limits.json`,
re-run the renderer, and open a pull request — the checker will confirm
your new value against upstream.

| subrequests per invocation | 50 — Subrequests to internal services (KV, D1, R2) have their own, larger budget of 1,000. |
| simultaneous outgoing connections | 6 — Relevant when proxying to several model APIs at once. |
| environment variables | 64/Worker — 5 KB per value. |
| worker size | 64 MiB |
| worker startup time | 1 second |
| workers per account | 100 |
| cron triggers per account | 5 |
| request body size | 100 MB — Set by the Cloudflare account plan, not by the Workers plan. |
| response body size | No enforced limit — Response body size is not capped by the Workers plan. |
<!-- limits:end workers -->

**10 ms of CPU is not "10 ms of wall clock".** Time spent waiting on a
network socket is not CPU time. So `await fetch("https://api.gemini...")`
costs almost nothing even when the model takes eight seconds to answer.
What *does* cost CPU is work: JSON parsing, string manipulation, crypto,
serialisation.

The consequence is concrete:

```ts
// Wrong. Buffers the whole response, then parses a large JSON body.
// A multi-megabyte response will blow the 10 ms budget.
const res = await fetch(url, { headers });
const data = await res.json();
return Response.json(data);

// Right. Piping the body through costs almost no CPU.
return new Response(res.body, {
  headers: { "content-type": "text/event-stream" },
});
```

Stream. Do not buffer. Parse only what you must.

### Durable Objects — the escape hatch

<!-- limits:begin durable_objects -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| max classes per account | 100 (Free) — Workers Paid allows 500. |
| storage per account | 5GB (Free) — Unlimited on Workers Paid. Storage is measured in GB (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes), not GiB. |
| storage per durable object | 10 GB |
| number of objects | Unlimited — Within an account or of a given class. |
| cpu per request | 30 seconds (default) — This is the escape hatch from the 10 ms Worker limit: every incoming request or WebSocket message resets the CPU budget to 30 seconds, configurable up to 5 minutes of active CPU time. |
| websocket message size | 32 MiB — Applies to received messages only. |
| key value size | 2 MB — Key and value combined. |
| free tier reset | Daily free limits reset at 00:00 UTC — Free-tier Durable Object limits are daily, not monthly. |
| included requests per month | 1,000,000 — The included allocation on the Workers Paid plan. |
| included duration gb s per month | 400,000 GB-s — Duration is billed in GB-seconds: seconds multiplied by memory in GB. |
| price per million requests | $0.15 — Charged beyond the included allocation on Workers Paid. |
| pending io holds memory | 15 minutes — A pending I/O operation keeps the object resident, and billable, for up to 15 minutes. |
<!-- limits:end durable_objects -->

**Rule of thumb: if a request needs more than 10 ms of CPU, it belongs in a
Durable Object.** That covers stateful sessions, WebSocket servers, anything
doing real computation, and every realtime agent.

**Use the WebSocket Hibernation API.** A hibernating Durable Object is
evicted from memory between messages and restored on the next one, which
removes the duration charge for an idle agent session. An agent that waits
ten seconds for the user to speak is idle most of the time — hibernate it.

### D1 — the query budget

<!-- limits:begin d1 -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| databases per account | 10 (Free) — Workers Paid allows 50,000. |
| max database size | 500 MB (Free) — Workers Paid allows 10 GB. |
| max storage per account | 5 GB (Free) — Workers Paid allows 1 TB. |
| queries per worker invocation | 50 (Free) — Workers Paid allows 1,000. This is the D1-specific budget: a free Worker may only issue 50 D1 queries per request, so batch reads into a single call instead of looping. |
| time travel retention | 7 days — Point-in-time recovery window. Workers Paid allows 30 days. |
| max row size | 2,000,000 bytes (2 MB) — Maximum string, BLOB or table row size. |
| max sql statement length | 100,000 bytes (100 KB) |
| max bound parameters | 100 |
| max query duration | 30 seconds |
| max restore operations | 10 restores per 10 minutes — Per database. |
<!-- limits:end d1 -->

Fifty queries per invocation is the number that catches people. A loop that
reads twenty conversations one at a time is already at 40% of the budget
before it does anything else.

```ts
// Wrong: N round trips, each one counting against the 50-query budget.
const rows = [];
for (const id of ids) {
  rows.push(await env.DB.prepare("SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?").bind(id).first());
}

// Right: one statement, one round trip.
const { results } = await env.DB.prepare(
  `SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (${ids.map(() => "?").join(",")})`
).bind(...ids).all();
```

### KV — reads are cheap, writes are not

<!-- limits:begin kv -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| reads per day | 100,000 reads per day |
| writes to different keys per day | 1,000 writes per day — The asymmetry with reads is the trap: reading a cached value is cheap, persisting state is not. Use KV as a cache, not as a database. |
| writes to same key | 1 per second — Applies to every plan. |
| storage per account | 1 GB |
| storage per namespace | 1 GB |
| value size | 25 MiB |
| key size | 512 bytes |
| operations per invocation | 1000 |
| namespaces per account | 1,000 |
| minimum cache ttl | 30 seconds — The smallest value you can pass to cacheTtl. |
<!-- limits:end kv -->

One thousand writes per day, and one write per second to the same key.
Any design where a Durable Object writes conversation state to KV on every
turn will hit the per-second ceiling within a minute of real traffic. Keep
session state inside the Durable Object, and use KV only for things you
read far more often than you write.

### R2 — free egress

<!-- limits:begin r2 -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| storage | 10 GB-month / month — Billed on the average peak storage per day across the billing period. Standard storage only. |
| class a operations | 1 million requests / month — List, Put, Copy and similar metadata operations. |
| class b operations | 10 million requests / month — Get and similar read operations. |
| egress | Free — The reason to prefer R2 over S3 on a free tier: there is no egress charge at all. |
| infrequent access storage | does not apply to Infrequent Access storage — The free tier covers Standard storage only. |
<!-- limits:end r2 -->

Free egress is the quiet superpower. Serving user uploads or model output
from R2 through a Worker costs nothing per byte served, where the same
traffic from S3 does not.

### Queues — the only place with real CPU

<!-- limits:begin queues -->
| Limit | Free tier |
| --- | --- |
| queues per account | 10,000 per account |
| message size | 128 KB — Around 100 bytes of that is internal metadata. |
| message retries | 100 |
| max consumer batch size | 100 messages |
| max send batch | 100 (or 256KB in total) |
| per queue throughput | 5,000 messages per second |
| message retention | Configurable up to 14 days |
| per queue backlog | 25GB |
| concurrent consumer invocations | 250 push-based only |
| consumer wall clock duration | 15 minutes |
| consumer cpu time | Configurable to 5 minutes — A queue consumer gets far more CPU time than an ordinary Worker. Run heavy work here rather than in the request path. |
| visibility timeout | 12 hours — Pull-based queues. |
| delay seconds | 24 hours — When sending or retrying. |
<!-- limits:end queues -->

A queue consumer gets **5 minutes of CPU** against a Worker's 10 ms. That
is a 30,000x difference. Anything heavy — embedding a batch of documents,
scraping and summarising a feed, transcoding media — belongs in a queue
consumer, not in the request handler and not in a Durable Object.

### Workers AI — inference with no API key

| Limit | Free tier |

| price per 1000 neurons | $0.011 per 1,000 Neurons — On the Workers Paid plan, above the free allocation. |
| text generation requests per minute | 300 requests per minute — Unless the model requires the Workers Paid plan. |

| summarization requests per minute | 1500 requests per minute |
| image to text requests per minute | 720 requests per minute |
| asr requests per minute | 720 requests per minute |
| object detection requests per minute | 3000 requests per minute |

| paid only models | @cf/moonshotai/kimi-k2.6, @cf/moonshotai/kimi-k2.7-code, @cf/zai-org/glm-5.2, @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3, @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash, @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731, @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017, and @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-pro-0813 — These require a Workers Paid plan or prepaid AI Gateway credits, so they are not available on a strictly free account. Workers AI is the fastest possible path to a working AI service: no
provider account, no API key, no card. Bind it and call it.

```ts
export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env) {
    const response = await env.AI.run(
      "@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct",
      { messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Hello" }] }
    );
    return Response.json(response);
```

## The workflow

Work through these in order. Each step has a decision point, and each
decision point has one right answer for a free tier.

### 1. Write down what is actually free

Before anything else, name the four numbers that will decide success:

- **Requests per day** the service must survive
- **CPU per request** the work needs
- **State that must persist** and how much of it
- **Realtime or not** — this decides Durable Objects

If the CPU number exceeds 10 ms, you are done: use a Durable Object or a
queue consumer. No amount of cleverness changes that.

### 2. Scaffold

```bash
npm create cloudflare@latest my-ai-service
cd my-ai-service
npx wrangler login
```

Pin the runtime and set the compatibility date so a future Workers release
cannot silently change behaviour:

```toml
# wrangler.toml
name = "my-ai-service"
main = "src/index.ts"
compatibility_date = "2026-10-22"
compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"]
```

### 3. Add the bindings you will actually use

Only add what you use. Every binding costs part of a budget.

```toml
[[d1_databases]]
binding = "DB"
database_name = "my-ai-service"
database_id = "<created by wrangler d1 create my-ai-service>"

[[r2_buckets]]
binding = "FILES"
bucket_name = "my-ai-service-files"

[[kv_namespaces]]
binding = "CACHE"
id = "<created by wrangler kv namespace create CACHE>"

[[queues.producers]]
binding = "TASKS"
queue = "my-ai-service-tasks"

[[queues.consumers]]
queue = "my-ai-service-tasks"
max_batch_size = 100
max_batch_timeout = 5

[[durable_objects.bindings]]
name = "SESSIONS"
class_name = "Session"

[[migrations]]
tag = "v1"
new_classes = ["Session"]

[ai]
binding = "AI"
```

### 4. Put the API key somewhere safe

```bash
npx wrangler secret put GEMINI_API_KEY
```

Secrets are encrypted at rest and are not readable from the dashboard. Never
put a key in a `define:` block, an env var checked into git, or the
frontend bundle. If the browser needs to call a model directly, proxy
through a Worker instead of exposing a key.

### 5. Stream the response

```ts
async function streamModel(prompt: string, apiKey: string): Promise<Response> {
  const upstream = await fetch(GEMINI_URL, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json", "x-goog-api-key": apiKey },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      contents: [{ parts: [{ text: prompt }] }],
      generationConfig: { maxOutputTokens: 512 },
    }),
  });

  if (!upstream.ok || !upstream.body) {
    return new Response("upstream error", { status: 502 });
  }

  // Pipe. Do not buffer, do not parse.
  return new Response(upstream.body, {
    headers: {
      "content-type": "text/event-stream",
      "cache-control": "no-cache",
    },
  });
}
```

### 6. Add auth before you add features

An unauthenticated AI endpoint is a gift to someone else. Put it behind a
shared secret checked in the Worker, and put the secret in a Durable Object
or KV only if you need per-user state.

```ts
function authorized(request: Request, env: Env): boolean {
  const header = request.headers.get("authorization") ?? "";
  return header === `Bearer ${env.API_TOKEN}`;
}
```

### 7. Rate-limit before you are rate-limited

Two enforcement points, and they catch different abuse:

- **Cloudflare WAF rate-limiting rules** for per-IP floods at the edge
- **Application-level counters** for per-key or per-account quotas

For an application-level counter on a free tier, keep it in a Durable
Object rather than KV — KV allows one write per second to the same key,
which a burst will exceed immediately.

### 8. Move slow work off the request path

```ts
// In the request handler: enqueue and return.
await env.TASKS.send({ jobId, kind: "summarise" });

// In the queue consumer: do the heavy thing.
export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env): Promise<Response> {
    const batch = await request.json() as MessageBatch<Task>;
    for (const message of batch.messages) {
      await summarise(message.body);
      message.ack();
    }
    return new Response("ok");
  },
};
```

### 9. Watch the budget, not the deployment

A free tier does not fail loudly. It silently returns 1027 at 00:00 UTC, or
starts rejecting writes, and you find out from a user. Check the Workers
dashboard for request counts and CPU, and set a cron trigger to alert
yourself.

```toml
[triggers]
crons = ["0 * * * *"]
```

### 10. Verify it is still free

Before you call it done, check the four numbers again against real usage:

- Requests per day, measured
- CPU per request, measured
- Storage, measured
- Writes to the same key, measured

A deployment that is free on day one and bills you on day two is worse than
one that never shipped.

## Traps

**Buffering a streaming response.** The single most common mistake. It
turns a 10 ms budget into a multi-second one and breaks streaming for the
user. Pipe the body.

**Treating CPU time as wall-clock time.** Waiting on a socket is free. A
`while` loop over a large array is not. `JSON.parse` of a multi-megabyte
body is not.

**Using KV as a database.** One thousand writes per day and one write per
second per key. Use D1.

**Issuing D1 queries in a loop.** Fifty per invocation. Batch them.

**Running heavy work in the request handler.** Move it to a queue consumer
and get 5 minutes of CPU instead of 10 ms.

**Ignoring hibernation for realtime sessions.** An agent session that sits
idle between turns is billed for the whole session. Hibernation removes
that.

**Putting a provider API key in the frontend.** It is in the bundle, it is
public, and it will be used by someone else. Proxy through a Worker.

**Exposing a Durable Object class per user.** You get 100 classes on the
free tier, not 100,000 objects. Use one class, one object per user id.

**Assuming the free tier will last.** Verify the limits against the live
documentation before you quote a number to anyone. This skill's own limits
are checked by a harness in CI; do the same for anything you assert.

**Shipping without a README.** A deployment someone cannot run is not a
deployment. Write the setup steps, the environment variables, and one
working example.

# Streaming proxy

A Cloudflare Worker that streams a model response and enforces a shared
token. Part of the [shipfree](../../README.md) skill.

## Deploy

```bash
npm install
npx wrangler secret put GEMINI_API_KEY
npx wrangler secret put API_TOKEN
npm run deploy
```

## Call it

```bash
curl -N https://shipfree-streaming-proxy.<you>.workers.dev \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello in one sentence."}]}'
```

The response arrives as server-sent events. `-N` disables curl's output
buffering so you see the stream as it happens.

## What it demonstrates

| Decision | Why |
| --- | --- |
| The upstream body is piped, not buffered | A free Worker gets 10 ms of CPU. Waiting on a socket is not CPU time; parsing a large JSON body is. |
| The API key is a Worker secret | A key in the bundle is a public key. |
| Rate limiting uses a Durable Object | KV allows one write per second to the same key; a burst exceeds that instantly. |
| Auth runs before the upstream call | An unauthenticated AI endpoint is a gift to someone else. |

## Local development

```bash
cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars   # fill in both values
npm run dev
```

# Contributing to shipfree

Thank you for taking the time. This project exists because free-tier limits
are scattered, phrased misleadingly, and change without warning. Every
contribution either fixes a number or improves the guidance around it.

## The most useful contribution: a drifted limit

If you find a limit in the skill that is wrong, outdated, or missing, that
is the highest-value change you can make.

**Do not edit the table in `SKILL.md` by hand.** The tables are generated.
Instead:

1. Open an issue with the upstream documentation link and the correct value,
   or go straight to a pull request.
2. Edit `limits.json` with the new value.
3. Regenerate the tables:

   ```bash
   python harness/fetch_limits.py --refresh
   python harness/check_limits.py
   python harness/render_skill.py
   ```

4. Run `make check`. The checker will confirm your new value against
   upstream, so a wrong fix fails before it merges.

If a limit moved to a different documentation page, update the platform's
`doc` path in `limits.json` at the same time.

## Adding a platform

1. Add an entry under `limits` in `limits.json`.
2. If the platform's documentation is published as source, point `doc` at it
   and add it to `harness/fetch_limits.py`'s source map. If it is not, leave
   `doc` as `null` — the checker will report the values as `skipped` rather
   than silently passing them.
3. Add the platform to `platform_matrix`.
4. Run `make render` and `make check`.

## Adding a skill

The repository holds one flagship skill today. If you want to add a second:

- Put it in `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
- Add the same frontmatter shape: `name`, `description`, `license`.
- The description is what an agent reads to decide whether to load the skill.
  Write it for that decision, not for a human reading a README.
- Mirror the file into `.opencode/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and update
  `tests/test_manifests.py`.

## Style

- Python: standard library only for the harness. No runtime dependencies.
- Type hints on public functions, docstrings that explain *why*.
- Conventional Commits: `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `chore:`,
  `style:`, `refactor:`.

## Development

```bash
make check
```

That runs the unit tests, the manifest consistency checks, the skill
renderer check, and the limit verification against upstream.

## Code of conduct

By participating you agree to abide by the
[Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

# Roadmap

## Now

- [x] The `shipfree` skill with machine-verified free-tier limits
- [x] A limits harness that checks `limits.json` against upstream documentation
- [x] A generator that renders the skill's tables from `limits.json`
- [x] Plugin manifests for twelve agent harnesses
- [x] A streaming-proxy template
- [ ] An agent-api template (Worker + D1 + Durable Object + Queue)

## Next

- [ ] **More platforms.** Vercel, Netlify, Hugging Face Spaces, Render and
      Fly.io currently have no machine-readable upstream source, so their
      limits are hand-verified and marked `skipped` by the checker. Finding
      or building a fetchable source for each would move them to verified.
- [ ] **A `vercel` source.** Vercel's limits page is rendered from a
      Next.js app. A small parser for its embedded data would let the
      checker verify it like the rest.
- [ ] **A second template.** A full agent API: Worker + D1 for conversation
      history, a Durable Object for the session, a queue consumer for
      embeddings.
- [ ] **A cost estimator.** Given requests/day, CPU/request, storage and
      egress, compute whether a given architecture stays inside the free
      tier and where it breaks first.
- [ ] **A preflight check.** A command that inspects a `wrangler.toml` and
      warns about bindings the project does not need, missing
      `compatibility_date`, a provider key exposed in the frontend bundle, or
      a request handler doing work that belongs in a queue.

## Later

- [ ] **A second skill.** The format supports a bundle. Candidates:
      a `selfhost` skill for running models locally, or a `llm-cost` skill
      for shaving token spend.
- [ ] **Per-harness installation docs.** A script that detects which harness
      is running and prints the exact install command for it.
- [ ] **A drift dashboard.** A public page showing when each limit was last
      verified, so users can judge how fresh the data is.
- [ ] **Model-provider free tiers.** Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter and
      Hugging Face Inference have their own free allowances that change on
      their own schedule. Covering them needs a different verification
      approach, since their documentation is not published as source.

## Explicitly not planned

- **A hosted deployment service.** shipfree is a skill, not a product.
- **Paid features.** The whole point is that the guidance is free and
  verifiable.

# Security Policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please report security issues privately rather than opening a public issue.

Open a [private security advisory](https://github.com/AryanRajMaurya/shipfree/security/advisories/new)
on this repository, or contact the maintainer directly. Include:

- What the issue is
- Steps to reproduce it
- The impact you believe it has

You can expect an acknowledgement within a few days and a fix or an
explanation of why a fix is not appropriate.

## Scope

This repository ships **documentation and templates**. It is not a service,
and it does not handle credentials in production.

That said, two classes of issue are taken seriously:

### 1. Insecure templates

The templates in `templates/` are starting points that people deploy
unchanged. A template that ships with a hardcoded secret, a permissive CORS
policy, an unauthenticated mutating endpoint, or a missing rate limit is a
vulnerability in this repository, because the first person to copy it
inherits the problem.

### 2. Wrong guidance

If the skill instructs an agent to do something insecure — putting a provider
API key in a frontend bundle, disabling authentication to "make the demo
work", running a shell command with unvalidated input — that is a
vulnerability. The skill is read by agents that write code other people
deploy.

## Non-vulnerabilities

- The repository does not run code from the internet as part of its normal
  operation, apart from the documentation fetch in `harness/`, which only
  reads public documentation.
- Reports about upstream platforms' own limits or pricing are not
  vulnerabilities here. If a limit is wrong, that is a documentation issue
  — open a normal issue.
- Reports about a template requiring configuration the user did not supply
  (such as an unset API key) are configuration issues, not vulnerabilities.

## Supported versions

The `main` branch is supported. Published releases are supported until the
next one.

# Shipfree

When the goal is to deploy an AI service for free, load the `shipfree` skill
from `.agents/skills/shipfree/SKILL.md` and follow it. It carries the
machine-verified free-tier limits and the architecture that fits inside them.

The four rules that cause most free-tier failures:

1. **Cloudflare Workers Free gets 10 ms of CPU per invocation.** Time waiting
   on a socket is not CPU time, so streaming a model response is cheap.
   Buffering and parsing a large JSON body is not. Pipe response bodies; do
   not buffer them.
2. **Durable Objects get 30 seconds of CPU per request.** Anything needing
   real CPU, per-user state, or WebSockets belongs in a Durable Object, not a
   Worker. Use the WebSocket Hibernation API so idle sessions are not billed.
3. **D1 allows 50 queries per Worker invocation.** Batch reads into one
   statement instead of looping. KV allows only 1,000 writes per day and one
   write per second per key, so KV is a cache, never a database.
4. **Queue consumers get 5 minutes of CPU.** Move embedding, summarising,
   scraping and transcoding off the request path into a queue consumer.

Never put a provider API key in the frontend. Proxy through a Worker and
keep the key in `wrangler secret put`.

Full limits, workflow and templates: `.agents/skills/shipfree/SKILL.md`.
